video_title: AI Design Still Feels Like a Slot Machine
gist: Canva's head of AI research explains why Canva trains its own small, vertically integrated design models (Canva Craft image model with scene-graph planning, Canva Brush design agent) that are ~40x cheaper than frontier models, arguing creative AI must be built around fast human-in-the-loop iteration. He highlights steep inference cost deflation (video generation down ~100x in a year), the ~100B-parameter sufficiency of LLMs for creative tasks, and fast-growing enterprise and agent/MCP demand for Canva's models via API.

insights.claim: Canva now runs roughly 100 AI models in production and launched a new model nearly every week in the month it debuted Canva Research (Canva Craft, then Canva Brush).
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Canva is becoming an AI model developer, not just an API consumer of frontier labs, which reduces its dependence on (and spend with) third-party model vendors.
insights.quote: we have a total of 100 AI models in production roughly right now

insights.claim: Canva's rationale for training its own models rests on two factors: proprietary design data nobody else has, and deep vertical integration of models into its product stack that yields large performance and cost gains; Kurazza expects many companies with thousands of employees or fewer to follow the same path.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Signals a broader trend of data-rich application companies building in-house models, a headwind for frontier-lab API revenue in vertical use cases and a tailwind for GPU cloud/inference tooling.
insights.quote: first of all you have unique data that nobody else has

insights.claim: Canva found that a model with two orders of magnitude fewer parameters, fine-tuned or trained on its unique data, can beat much larger general models on design tasks while being another order of magnitude faster and cheaper.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that proprietary data plus small specialized models can undercut frontier models on cost in narrow domains.
insights.quote: you can fine-tune or train a model that is two orders of magnitude fewer parameters if you have the data and you can beat the bigger model

insights.claim: Canva says its models are currently about 40x cheaper than the most expensive frontier models performing the same design task, at similar and sometimes better quality.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: A 40x cost gap on design tasks implies frontier labs face pricing pressure in vertical creative workloads.
insights.quote: right now we are in the you know 40x cheaper than like the most expensive frontier models that can do the same design task

insights.claim: Using the latest frontier LLM to drive image generation would cost on the order of a dollar per image, which Kurazza says makes the economics unworkable for mass creative use.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Unit economics, not capability, is the gating factor for AI in high-volume consumer creative tools.
insights.quote: it will be like a dollar per image generated or something like that

insights.claim: Canva Craft was trained from scratch because Canva believed several breakthroughs were not present in existing models, whereas Canva Brush (its vision language model) was built on top of an open-weights base model.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Shows a pragmatic build-vs-adapt approach; open-weights bases remain important to application-layer companies.

insights.claim: Canva's research roadmap is now planned only about a month ahead; none of the models it ships today were underway a year ago, and it expects to release models next year that it hasn't started on yet.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Rapid model obsolescence means competitive moats rest on data, distribution and iteration speed rather than any single model.
insights.quote: like a year ago none of the project the models that we ship now was underway

themes.theme: Iteration, control and the 'slot machine' problem

insights.claim: Kurazza argues that Silicon Valley wrongly expects new AI tech to be single-shot perfect; for creative tasks AI will get 70-80% of the way and never 100%, so products must be built around fast human-in-the-loop iteration.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Favors workflow/editor incumbents (where the last mile happens) over pure single-shot generation vendors.
insights.quote: AI will get 70% 80% there will never get to 100%

insights.claim: Pipelines where an image model generates, an LLM critiques, and the image model regenerates lose control and throw away information each loop; Canva Craft instead generates a scene graph first so an LLM or human can make non-destructive edits before pixels are rendered.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Structured, layered generation is a product differentiator versus flat-pixel image models for professional design workflows.

insights.claim: Canva Craft's pipeline has three steps: amplifying the prompt/context, converting it into a structured scene graph, and finally generating pixels with a from-scratch diffusion model; splitting the steps enables new agent workflows such as generating 10 layout plans for human approval before rendering.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Modular generation pipelines allow cheaper partial calls (layout only) and better agent integration.

insights.claim: Consistency and control are the two things creatives have asked AI for over the last two years, and Canva explicitly aims to avoid 'slot machine' generation where users regenerate 20 times hoping to get lucky.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Predictability is the axis on which professional design AI will compete, not raw aesthetic quality.
insights.quote: we don't want to provide slot machines you know we're like hey if you generate 20 times you may get lucky

insights.claim: The majority of images processed by Canva's Magic Layers feature, which decomposes flat images into editable layers and elements, come from outside Canva, i.e., generated elsewhere and brought into Canva for editing.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Canva captures value from competitors' image generators by owning the editing step, positioning it as a downstream aggregator.
insights.quote: the majority of images that we process with magic layers come from outside Canva

insights.claim: Speed is a game changer, not a nice-to-have: with fast models an LLM can run around 10 self-critique iterations on its own output before showing a human, which was infeasible when each iteration took a minute.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Inference speed directly converts into quality, making latency optimization a core competitive lever.
insights.quote: speed is not just a nice to have speed is like a complete game changer

insights.claim: Kurazza cites a game-development rule that anything taking more than 10 seconds is out of the question, and says Canva is targeting near-instantaneous AI because day-to-day users won't wait a minute for generation.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Latency thresholds determine everyday adoption; slower premium models may be relegated to niche use.
insights.quote: anything that takes more than 10 seconds is completely really out of the question

themes.theme: Data, training recipe and model scaling

insights.claim: Canva Craft ranked number four on Design Arena on its first submission, which Kurazza attributes to underestimating the power of a decade of Canva design data plus user data (with permission) and licensed data.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Proprietary vertical data can vault a newcomer near the top of public leaderboards quickly.
insights.quote: I think we we underestimated the the power of like a decade of design generated and design data that we had

insights.claim: Canva learned that diffusion models above a certain parameter size can absorb far more detailed, structured scene descriptions (bounding boxes, poses, relative positions), so its scene descriptions grew significantly over six months alongside a modestly larger diffusion model.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Quality gains are coming from co-designing the planner and renderer rather than scaling either alone.

insights.claim: Kurazza claims that for most creative tasks LLMs/VLMs of around 100 billion parameters suffice when well tuned, so the size of the language model feeding image/video generation is stabilizing rather than growing 10x every few months; video understanding may need slightly more.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Diminishing returns beyond ~100B parameters for creative workloads favor efficient, specialized models and weaken the case that frontier scale wins every vertical.
insights.quote: you don't need more than 100 billion parameter to do most of the creative tasks

insights.claim: Canva's training set mixes stock images, synthetic data, user-generated data and millions of designs Canva created or licensed over a decade, with heavy emphasis on diversity to avoid homogeneous 'AI slop' outputs for a global user base.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Licensed and owned data reduce IP risk and support differentiated aesthetics.

insights.claim: Canva Craft initially performed well on portraits and nature landscapes but underperformed on cartoons because effort to make portraits photorealistic bled into cartoons, making them too realistic and 3D; Canva treats this as a taste issue fixable via fine-tuning and RL rather than pre-training.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Style weaknesses in image models are cheap to fix post-training, so leaderboard category gaps may close quickly.

insights.claim: Image-generation benchmarks lag the real use of AI in design because they focus on single-shot generation; there is no established industry benchmark for how well a model edits an existing design, and PresentBench covers only around 200 presentation generation tasks.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Public leaderboards may misrank tools for professional editing workflows; an opportunity exists for design-editing benchmarks.
insights.quote: as of today there is no established benchmark for how good a model is at editing a design

insights.claim: Canva uses VLMs as judges with well-articulated rubrics (readability, layout, composition) and finds them quite reliable, supplemented by human evaluation; building them forced Canva to explicitly define what makes a design good.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Automated VLM evaluation lowers iteration cost for model training, accelerating vertical model development.

themes.theme: Canva Brush agent and harness design

insights.claim: Canva Brush is an agent that creates and edits heterogeneous designs (vector graphics, images, text) and can handle high-level directives like 'make it pop' or 'make it Gen Z', or build a cohesive on-brand 30-slide deck.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Moves Canva from tool provider toward an AI design agent, competing with general chatbots for design work.

insights.claim: Kurazza says the agent harness was the hardest part of building Canva Brush, now in its third generation, and the lesson was to make it thinner and simpler, removing encoded human knowledge so the LLM can run freely using code to operate design tools.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: As base models improve, value shifts from heavy scaffolding to data and tools; thin-harness designs age better.
insights.quote: the importance of the harness cannot be cannot be overstated

insights.claim: Canva chose representations for design editing operations based on what is best represented in LLM training data, aligning with existing model capabilities rather than teaching out-of-distribution formats.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Products that express their operations in code-like, well-represented formats will get more leverage from each new frontier model.

insights.claim: Until about a year ago LLMs were blind to their own output; the ability for LLMs to see what they generate and iterate is what changed everything for design agents.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Multimodal self-verification is the key enabler for agentic creative tools.

themes.theme: Inference cost deflation and full-stack optimization

insights.claim: Kurazza says AI inference optimization is very early: Canva engineers can get 10x improvements in a month and 5x speedups in two weeks, implying the cost curve is far from plateauing.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Continued steep inference cost declines will expand AI usage among free users and compress pricing for generation services.
insights.quote: if you can squeeze 10x performance improvement in a month means you're very early

insights.claim: The cost of generating a second of 720p AI video fell about two orders of magnitude in roughly a year, from around half a dollar to sub-cent per second.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Rapid deflation in video generation costs undermines premium pricing for video-gen vendors and expands addressable use cases.
insights.quote: now you can generate sub cent where like uh a year ago it was like half a dollar uh per second of generation

insights.claim: Kurazza predicts another order-of-magnitude cost decline, and argues reaching about 0.1 cent per generated image or second of video would be another breakthrough for democratization, though he does not expect inference to become as cheap as storage.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Watch for price points near $0.001 per output as a trigger for mass-market AI creative adoption.
insights.quote: when you get to like 0.1 cent per generated image or generated second of video, I think it's another breakthrough

insights.claim: Canva optimizes everything except owning hardware: it runs models on cloud GPU instances and tunes kernels, step reduction, distillation, batching, caching and serving; Kurazza says real efficiency requires owning the full stack and having access to model weights.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Companies with weight access (own or open-weights models) gain cost advantages over those renting closed APIs.
insights.quote: you can only make it really efficient if you own the full stack

insights.claim: A wave of San Francisco startups (Kurazza could name about a dozen) is focused on inference optimization, often founded by graphics and cloud engineers, because the ROI pitch of cutting inference cost by ~10x is simple and AI adoption is creating strong cost-reduction pressure.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Inference-optimization is a hot startup category with easy-to-sell ROI; potential acquisition targets for clouds and AI labs.
insights.quote: there is so much money left on the table right now

insights.claim: Canva plans distilled 'Craft Fast' and 'Craft Ultrafast' variants within weeks, with the LLM and diffusion components distilled jointly; cheaper variants may become the default for prototypes while the full model is used for quality.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Tiered model pricing expands Canva's API addressable market among cost-sensitive developers.

insights.claim: Free users make up the majority of Canva's users, and lowering inference costs is explicitly what lets Canva extend more AI to students and nonprofits on the free tier.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Inference cost reductions are a lever on Canva's freemium funnel and margins.

themes.theme: Open-weights dynamics in image vs video

insights.claim: About four months ago some video-model developers began releasing open-weights versions, triggering a domino effect that forced competitors to follow; now most top image models are closed while video models are increasingly open weights.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Open-weights competition in video compresses pricing power for closed video-gen vendors.

insights.claim: Kurazza links the open-weights wave in video to plummeting cost per second of AI video, because a broad community can work on cracking efficiency when weights are available.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Expect faster cost deflation in open-weight modalities; closed-model moats are weaker there.

themes.theme: Agents as customers: API and MCP distribution

insights.claim: Canva Craft is now accessible via the Canva MCP server and the Canva Connect API, and Canva reports MCP usage on its platform is skyrocketing.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Canva is positioning itself as a design tool layer invoked by third-party AI agents, opening an API/usage-based revenue line.
insights.quote: we are seeing like uh the usage of of MCP on camera like really skyrocket

insights.claim: Canva's enterprise business is its fastest-growing segment with triple-digit year-over-year growth, and enterprise customers are driving demand for API access to build custom workflows.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Enterprise strength is a key metric for Canva's valuation and any future IPO narrative.
insights.quote: our enterprise business is the fastest growing business that we have

insights.claim: Demand for Canva's model APIs comes from two groups: enterprises building custom (vibe-coded) workflows, and users of chat assistants like Claude or ChatGPT whose agents call Canva via MCP and then hand off to Canva for editing.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Chat assistants may become a distribution channel for Canva rather than a pure substitute.

insights.claim: Kurazza believes building for agents, not just humans, is unavoidable; agents need structured documentation, low-friction trials without credentials or upfront purchase, and the ability to test before recommending to a human because agents increasingly choose which solution to use.
insights.speaker: Stephano Kurazza (head of AI research, Canva)
insights.so_what: Software vendors that reduce agent onboarding friction may win share as agents become the purchase decision-makers.
insights.quote: many times it will be the agent that will decide what solution to use
